doc.title: Burrill Crohn interviewed by Monk Rowe, Woodstock, New York, January 3, 2012

title: Pitching a history of jazz and making Women in Jazz for A&E
summary: With no film experience he pitched David Chertok and A&E, ended up making Women in Jazz, and learned as he went.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Was there a model for you? Things to look at?

No. I mean the more I started doing it the more I looked at other people’s work. But I’ll just finish, so I happened to know someone at what was then called ABC Video Enterprises, which was the forerunner of Arts & Entertainment Network. And I went to them — I think I contacted David Chertok, the film collector. I saw an article about him in the New York Times. And I went to him and I said, “David, let’s do a history of jazz series together.” It was very bold, I’d never made a film. Oh I take it back, I take it back. So I went to this guy and I said I wanted to do a history of jazz series. Come to think of it I had contacted David, and I even gave him, which was silly, a deposit, like an advance against some of the work so that he wouldn’t work with anybody else, he’d do this with me. And then I went to A&E, this guy I knew, and I said, “Let’s do a history of jazz series.” And he went to his bosses. And at this time, it was very interesting — A&E during the day broadcasts women’s programming — beauty shows, health shows. And at night they did cultural programs. So their bosses came back to me and said, “How about doing a women in jazz series?” And I knew a lot about jazz but I didn’t really know about women in jazz but I figured I’ll find out. So I said okay, I’ll do that. And that led to the first thing I did which was a series of “Women in Jazz” narrated by Marian McPartland for the instrumental side, and Carmen McRae for the vocal side. And that played for a long time. But I didn’t know what I was doing. I learned as I went along. Remember Billy Rigo? He came with me to the Joe Williams shoot?
He was on board for that.

Billy — I showed him the clip of Wynton Marsalis, he was directing that shoot. And I remember saying, “Billy, what’s time code?” I didn’t even know what time code was when I started. But somehow I bluffed my way through and it came out okay. And I wrote them and I produced them and I directed them, and blah-blah-blah. So I just had this vision that this was what I wanted to do, and I learned as I went along.
